articles.text: Editor: My family and I were beyond ecstatic when the announcement was released that a BIPOC female Assistant Principal from Miramonte High School was chosen to lead Piedmont High School. After a brief review of Ms. Sukanya Goswami’s limited online credentials and statistical research of her previous schools of leadership employment, I asked myself, “Were the other applicants for the PHS principal position coming from schools with even lower proficiency scores?” For example, at Westmoor High School in Daly City, 61% of its students scored at or above the state’s reading level but only 44% of its students in the math segment. Is this the road our students are headed? articles.text: The Diversity Film series continues with a screening of Power to Heal on May 5. The event is being co-hosted by the City of Piedmont, Adult Education Program, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee (PADC). A Zoom webinar will feature The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. The hour-long documentary movie describes the history of segregated hospitals and a brief summary of civil rights activism to the internal workings of the federal government that led to integrated hospitals and African American access to health care. It narrates the early days of health inequity, powerfully demonstrating how race and poverty denied African Americans equal access to healthcare. Included are interviews that reveal personal experiences of African Americans’ struggles with illness and death without adequate healthcare. The film transitions from these individual stories to a broader review of disparities in hospital care throughout the United States. Physicians, civil rights leaders, and historians recount the dangerous tasks of documenting egregious incidents, tracking down patients, and the risks of blacks and whites working together to put desegregated structures in place. Following the screening, viewers will hear from Dr. Neil Powe, a leader in Public Health and the ongoing effort to correct healthcare disparities. Dr. Powe is a Harvard-trained physician, a professor of medicine at UCSF, and Chief of Medicine at San Francisco General Hospital. Viewers will hear from him about the history and current-day status of healthcare and will be able to ask him questions after the screening. To stream The Power to Heal, and for the conversation on zoom with Dr. Neil Powe from 6 p.m. to 7 p.m. on Thursday, May 5, click on diversityfilmseries.org. The streaming link for The Power to Heal will be active from May 2 through 5. Dr. Neil Powe is the guest speaker on May 5.

articles.text: April 19 marks first public meeting on the draft housing plan The ad-hoc Housing Advisory Committee, tasked with providing feedback on Piedmont’s 6th cycle Housing Element, received an informational report on the process thus far at its meeting on April 19. Members of the committee offered comments following a presentation by Lisa Wise Consulting, the firm hired by the city to guide the process. The Housing Advisory Committee was created by Piedmont City Council in 2021 to review and provide feedback on documents related to the housing element and programs, and meets as needed throughout the planning process. Feedback from its members will be considered by the Planning Commission and City Council when finalizing the element. The committee consists of Planning Commission Chair Rani Batra, June Catalano, Jane Lin, Justin Osler, and Claire Parisa. The Housing Element serves as an opportunity for community conversation on how to address long-standing housing challenges at the local level. It is meant to address various issues related to housing, including affordability, design, density, and site locations that could sustain more housing. “Although we are a small town, our [housing opportunity] sites are so unique, and the circumstances and opportunities for building is unique. So you need a long ‘menu’ to figure out what combination will work to make a site productive in terms of generating additional housing,” Batra said. Committee members offered comments on what goals and programs could be utilized to increase Piedmont’s housing stock. “It will be important to develop ways to make Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU) more affordable” Catalano said. “We will hopefully follow-up by including more detailed ways on how to do that in the Draft Housing Element.” She added that financial incentives for ADUs should provide for an increased number of units in Piedmont. ADUs have allowed Piedmont to meet its prior Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). However, the city will need to identify room for 587 new units, so the lion’s share of that allocation cannot be ADUs. Locations for multifamily units are being explored to help satisfy the RHNA. “We talked about the Corp. Yard and Blair Park as [possible locations] for low-income multifamily housing, but I’d like to see more specifics on Measure A-1 funding ($2.2 million) from the county that would support building for low- income housing,” Parisa said. The city has asked for a second extension of the use of Measure A-1 funds, approved by Alameda County voters in 2016, and is currently waiting for the Board of Supervisors to consider it at a public hearing. City Council authorized City Administrator Sara Lillevand to request the second extension. The city projects that City Council will review the Housing Element this summer, and the City will then submit it to the state for review in summer 2022. Piedmont is targeting a Housing Element 2023 - 2031 adoption by May 2023. Public comment may be given at an upcoming Planning Commission meeting on Monday, May 9 or Thursday, May 12, and by emailing PiedmontisHome@ piedmont.ca.gov. Use the interactive tool “Piedmont Housing Puzzle” to drop suggestions and comments on where the city can sustain new housing units. The FIRST Robotics Competition, which frames high school robotics as a full contact sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season and competitions start in the eighth week. In this year’s game, Rapid React, remotely controlled robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inchwide tennis balls into a funnel 8 feet high and 4 feet wide before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. Teams who qualify for the World Championship at regional tournaments in seven countries are placed into six divisions of 75. After 10 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners, the highest ranked eight teams become alliance captains and draft three others to work with throughout the double-elimination playoff brackets. articles.text: The Piedmont parent group ALPS (Advanced Learners Program Support) will host a meeting tomorrow night, Thursday, April 28, titled “Defining Academic Excellence in Today’s Learning Environment.” The meeting is ay 7 p.m. and will be held in the Piedmont High School Library. Michael Malone and Ella Grossberg are the co-presidents of ALPS. All Piedmont parents are invited to attend and learn how Piedmont School District can maintain its focus on academic excellence and ensure all students have access to rigorous, relevant, and engaging curriculum. articles.text: We all get stuck. You may not know how to finish a math problem, create a concluding paragraph, tabulate the earned income for the fiscal quarter or wash a white shirt with red stripes. But in school, and math and science particularly, getting stuck is not just a nuisance, it’s generally a sign that a student is approaching their subject matter inefficiently and ineffectively: relying on memory instead of logic. If students are stuck, they need to: 1) Get comfortable being stuck. 2) Know they can get past being stuck. 3) Follow the “unsticking” techniques. • You’re supposed to get stuck – a lot Too many students have a completely opposite mindset about being stuck. Here are all the things I get students to change in terms of their thinking about being stuck. • You’re supposed to get stuck. • Learn to be comfortable not being sure how to solve a problem. • You can figure this out. Trust yourself. I tell students to take a minute and become comfortable being unsure how to solve a problem. Just sit for a few seconds and don’t panic. Learn to transition from saying, “I don’t know what to do,” to saying, “I don’t know what to do, yet.” Once they are calm and comfortable with the idea that they can get themselves unstuck, we can move forward. • It’s time to start figuring things out If you can’t remember what the teacher taught you, know that it’s time to start figuring out how to solve the problem. Figuring out how to solve a problem is a completely different mindset than remembering what the teacher taught. Students need to change their mindset. • How to figure things out Here are some steps you can take to start figuring out how to solve a problem. • Don’t stop. • Re-read the question. Being stuck on a problem is a challenge to embrace. • • • • • Try anything and everything. Solve using logic. Write things down. Ask yourself whatever you would ask the teacher. Use multiple choice answers to your advantage. • Don’t stop: try anything and everything The most important rule is to never stop and never give up. It’s OK to try things even if you aren’t sure that they will get you the right answer. Just keep trying things and keep going. • Re-read the question strategically If you are stuck, it’s possible that you didn’t read the question correctly or missed some aspect of the question. So, the first thing you should do is to re-read the questions in a specific way: • Read every single word. Pretend you are reading it out loud to someone else. • Did you miss any part of the question the first time you read it? • Is there any part of the question that you haven’t used yet? • Write everything down The mind can process better when it can see what it is working with, so write everything down. • Equations: first write the equation, then re-write it with values. • Shapes and measurement: geometry is a visual process. Write down their values too, or a question mark for those you don’t know What you are looking for?: Sometimes it helps to just see what you are looking for. • Start with what you want, nt what you are given Logical problem-solving involves thinking about what information the question is asking for and thinking about what you need in order to get that answer. Memory involves thinking about what data you are given and trying to remember what you have been taught to do with that. Focus on what they want and what you need to get that. Then look at the problem for what you need. It’s there, go find it. • Ask yourself what you would ask the teacher You know how you can ask the teacher a question, and halfway through asking you figure out what you need to solve the problem? Well, be the teacher. Ask yourself whatever you would ask the teacher and try to answer your own questions. • Use multiple-choice answers If you are taking a multiple-choice test, the answer choices can help. articles.text: Inventive and creative spirit filled the high school campus at the Piedmont School Maker Faire on the Sunday, April 24, a beautiful afternoon. Piedmont Makers hosted the 8th Annual Riveropolis, an interactive nature play experience that was recently featured at the California Academy of Sciences, provided Makers the opportunity to build and race boats made of cork, wood and rubber bands. Faire, with over 80 Makers displaying a varied array of work at an event that attracted more than 1,200 people. The Faire celebrates K-12 Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Math (STEAM) education. Hands-on opportunities abounded at the Faire. Outdoor demonstrations filled the high school Quad, and the new STEAM building’s outdoor area. Crowd favorites Rocket Zone and Nerdy Derby were continuously surrounded by dozens of Makers, designing, hammering, hot gluing, decorating, and iterating their rockets and race cars. Student and community Makers exhibited projects across the spectrum. PHS junior Max Schleuning built and programmed an impressive Golf Launch Monitor that allowed guests to test the flight path from their swings. Middle School teacher Laura Archer hosted the Earthquake Shake Table Challenge, providing young engineers the opportunity to build structures and test whether they could support weights and remain standing through an earthquake. Sixth grader Ben Fisher and grandfather Gene Switkes designed and constructed a magnetic ball-bearing controlled lemonade dispenser mounted on a custom wooden stand. At the elementary school level, Beach 4th grader Ethan Grossberg shared his knowledge on cancer-fighting Turkey Tail mushrooms, and Wildwood 5th grader Evan Yamanaka crafted an Ocean Diorama using clay and epoxy resin. Havens 1st grader Jacob Dickinson and his father Robert taught visitors how to make electric cars powered by batteries or solar panels. Makers explored chemistry through creating their own scented Bath Fizzies with Piedmont Education Foundation volunteers. Wildwood students William Bridges and Jack Shim teamed up with mom Margaret Bridges to teach people how to build Marshmallow Shooters, and then test their aim. The Faire showcased the thriving Piedmont Robotics community with representation from all four robotics leagues. The Piedmont Highlanders team qualified for the FIRST Robotics Competition World Championships in Houston and advanced to the semi-finals. They shared videos from their season. FIRST Tech Challenge teams constructed an arena in the STEAM Engineering Patio and allowed guests to test drive their Freight Frenzy robots. Macron was distrusted, a turncoat on the environment, cost of living, and major issues: workers might stay home in the runoff. For the once powerful Socialist party, this presidential election had proved devastating: it was disheveled and splintered into six parties. Mélenchon, a significant player in the National Assembly, was the preferred candidate to oppose Macron, not Le Pen. Disappointingly, Mélenchon trailed by just slightly more than one point. She borrowed another $10 million in 2022 from Hungary helped by Viktor Orbán, the ruling despot soundly in Putin’s orbit. Le Pen was unwavering, but Macron scored. While Le Pen disapproves of Russia’s Ukraine invasion, she declines to fault Putin. Russia’s bloody atrocities against Ukraine disrupt world peace, and they warn that a Le Pen presidency could pursue Frexit where France exits the EU in a scenario Le Pen has described since 2010.

articles.text: WACC singles, doubles tourney this week Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team clinched another league championship after being undefeated in the Western Alameda County Conference. They defeated league opponent Castro Valley 6-1 on Monday, April 25 at home, but lost to North Coast Section rival Lick Wilmerding 4-3 in San Francisco on Wednesday, April 20. The Highlanders finished their regular season with a 13-4 overall record and perfect 10-0 against league opponents. Postseason play starts with the WACC Singles and Doubles Tournament this Friday and Saturday, April 29-30 at Chabot College in Hayward. Charlie Lambert and Lenni Burchardt will play singles. The doubles teams will include Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Olcott, the team’s No. 1 doubles pair all season, along with Ben Breber and Monte Imburg. Coach Jim Landes has requested bringing a third doubles team as well. “Charlie and Lenni will be playing singles. In doubles we have Kai and Charlie Olcott and Ben Breber and Monte Imburg. I feel confident that we’re going to do very well at doubles, we may even get an all-Piedmont doubles finals. Singles will be tough, but we can beat them,” said Landes. 6-1 win over Castro Valley Piedmont won three of four singles matches and all three doubles against the Trojans. In singles Breber won at No. 2 in three sets, 3-6, 6-2, 7-5. At No 3, Baudendistel won 6-2, 6-4, and Olcott at No. 4 singles won 6-3, 6-1. Burchardt lost 6-4, 6-4 at No. 1. In doubles, Pham and Imburg paired at No. 1 to win 6-3, 6-0. The No. 2 pair of Oliver Maxwell and Brady Colbert won by forfeit, and Charlie Sullivan and at No. 3, Carson Hicks won easily, 6-3, 6-1. 4-3 loss to Lick Playing in San Francisco, the storied rivalry with host Lick Wilmerding continued, as PHS lost two of the four singles matches and two of three doubles matches. Staff Photos Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel will play as a doubles team in the league championship tournament. Ben Breber will be paired with Monte Imburg in doubles. Burchardt won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 1 singles, and Baudendistel at No. 4 pulled out a gritty victory at No. 4, winning 7-6 (6-1), 7-5. Breber at No. 2 lost 6-4, 6-1, and Pham at No. 3 lost 6-2, 6-1 In doubles, Olcott and Imburg lost at No. 1 in three sets, 6-3, 2-6, 10-4. At No. 2, Maxwell and Colbert won 6-0, 6-2. At No. 3, Sullivan and Graham McWeeny won the first set, but McWeeny suffered an injury and tried to play through, eventually losing 3-6, 7-6, 10-7. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-4 overall, 10-0 league) heads to Chabot College for the WACC Individual Tournament this Friday and Saturday, April 29-30. Matches start on both days at 10:00 a.m. Charlie Lambert will play in the WACC singles bracket.

articles.text: Piedmont is finishing its track and field season with some record performances. Last week included their final league meet of the season at Castro Valley on Thursday, April 21, and an invitational, the Vikings Track Classic at Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa, on Saturday, April 23. The Highlanders will compete this Saturday, April 30, at the Clash of the Titans at Skyline High in Oakland, It will be the final meet prior to the WACC Championships on Saturday, May 7. All post-season meets will be held at Hayward High, other than the State Meet. WACC Meet The Highlanders won several events, and senior standout Parker Terrill improved his height in pole vault to 15-feet, 7-inches, another new school record. Terrill, who recently won the prestigious Del Campo Decathlon, also won the long jump with a personal record of 20feet, 5-inches in a field of 13. Additionally, Terrill won the 110- meter hurdles in 16.91 seconds and finished second of 20 sprinters in the 100 meters with a time of 11.96 seconds. Cooper Downing swept the half mile and mile races. He won the 800 meters in 2:02.39 in a field of 13 runners and won the 1600 meters with a time of 4:24.52 in a field of 19. Piedmont runners swept the 1600, with Downing, Jack Stein second, Parker Long third, and Christian Taylor fourth. Downing also ran the anchor leg of the 4x400 relay, won by Taylor, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Parker Long, and Downing in 3:40.58. The PHS boys’ 4x100 relay team of Quincy Munyan, Luke Alban, Russell Tan, and Matthew Riordan won with a time of 44.33 seconds. Ellie Black won the 1600 meters in 5:14.51, and Jamie Schwarz was in 5:39.52. Black also won the 3200 in 11:52.64, and Schwarz took second in the 800 in 2:28.30. Brie Sotelo won the shot put with a distance of 30-feet, 3.5-inches, and Sara Govert was third of at 24-feet, 11-inches. Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Parker Terrill won the pole vault, 110-meter hurdles, and placed second in the 100-meters at a league meet on April 21. Brie Sotelo won the shot put at a league meet with a throw of 30-feet, 3.5-inches. Sotelo also was second in the 100 hurdles in 18.19 seconds. The girls’ 4x100 relay team of Jasmyn Milsum, Breah Bell, Teresa McKay, and Ella Yasar won with a time of 53.62. Vikings Track Classic Piedmont brought seven student-athletes to the Vikings Track Classic in Santa Rosa. Top finishes include: Ellie Black: second of seven runners in the 3200 with a time of 10:58.56. Matthew Riordan was sixth of 75 sprinters in the 100 with a time of 11.43. Riordan was also sixth of 58 in the 200, timed in 23.96. In the 800, Zirkelbach-Ngai was 15th of 64 in 2:14.85. NEXT UP Piedmont heads to Skyline HS in Oakland this Saturday, April 30 for the Clash of the Titans. Events start at 9:00 a.m. Cooper Downing won the 800- and 1600-meters at a recent league meet.

articles.text: Staff Photos The PHS boys’ lacrosse team and coach Alex Yu look ahead to a rematch with Bishop O’Dowd in the league playoffs this week. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team split its last two games of the regular season, defeating Acalanes in overtime on Tuesday, April 19 in Lafayette, but losing to Novato 10-6 on Friday, April 22 at Witter Field. Both are considered top-level contenders in Division 2 of the North Coast Section. Piedmont was moved up to Div.1 in 2020 after winning the championship. “Novato and Acalanes are playing all Division 1 (opponents), and they are Div.2, explained Piedmont first-year head coach Alex Yu. “I’ve known Novato’s coach, Mike Hardy, since the old school, We played against each other back in 88’-89.” The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 7-7 overall, second to O’Dowd in the WACC with a 4-1 record against league opponents. The Dragons won their regular season match 13-7 on March 18. The Highlanders will receive a first-round bye as the No. 2 seed, and will play No. 3 Berkeley (12- 9) today, April 27 at 5:30 p.m. Witter Field is the host site for this year’s championship game on Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont has won every WACC Championship since entering the league in 2017 but faces stiff competition from a strong O’Dowd team. “We’ll see Berkeley on Wednesday and we don’t want to look past them. It’s one game at a time and we have to take care of business first,” said Yu. The Dragons enter the playoffs with the No. 1 seed for the first time since 2017. They defeated PHS 8-7 during the regular season, but the Highlanders went onto win the 2017 championship 9-8 in overtime. Yu was an assistant coach with O’Dowd on that team. 15-14 OT win over Acalanes It was a heated contest pm April 19 against the Dons of Acalanes. Piedmont trailed 5-4 by the end of the first quarter but went ahead 8-7 by halftime. The Dons stormed ahead with five goals in the third quarter to take a 12-10 lead. In the fourth quarter, PHS scored four goals to jump ahead, 14-13 with 1:21 left in the game. Acalanes tied the match with 36 seconds left to play to force overtime. In OT, the Highlanders were able to kill a 90-second penalty, and Jack Nelson scored the game-winner in the closing minutes. Midfielder Noah Lindenbaum was awarded the game ball after recording a pivotal clearance in overtime that changed possession and helped Piedmont win the game. Final stats: Nate Fredericks led with six goals and one assist. Soren Dixon had four goals and four assists. Spencer Settlemier scored twice. Jack Nelson had two goals and an assist. Rylan Nelson scored once. 10-6 loss to Novato Novato came out the gates with a 5-1 lead in the first quarter and 7-2 by halftime. Piedmont narrowed the score to 7-4 in the third period, but a 3-goal deficit was the closest it got, ending in a 10-6 win for Novato. Final stats: Fredericks scored twice with two ground balls. Dixon had a goal, assist, and a ground ball. Jack Nelson scored once with six ground balls. NEXT UP Piedmont (7-7 overall, 4-1 league) plays in the league semifinals against Berkeley on Wednesday, April 27 at 5:30 p.m. They will likely face Bishop O’Dowd in the WACC Championship game on Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. at Witter Field.

articles.text: Piedmont beats Acalanes 10-7, Berkeley 15-11 Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team finished up its regular season with a 10-7 win over Acalanes at Witter Field on Tuesday, April 19 and a 15-11 win at Berkeley in the season-finale on Friday, April 22. PHS record is now 8-8 overall and 3-1 against league opponents. They will enter the WACC Playoffs with the No. 2 seed, behind No. 1 Bishop O’Dowd for the first time since entering the league in 2017. It was the only year the Dragons won a WACC title. The Highlanders will face No. 3 Berkeley on Wednesday, April 27 at 7:00 p.m, in a playoff-double header with the boys’ team at Witter Field. The WACC Championship game will be hosted at Witter Field on Friday, April 29 at 7:00 p.m. Friday’s game against Berkeley was perhaps a sign of things to come. The game was a physical affair which included a Berkeley player being red carded (ejected from the game), and Piedmont picking up some knocks along the way. Coach Carlton Chan is hoping to temper emotions and keep referees attentive on fouls. “We’re getting the girls excited, it’s definitely a big week. Unfortunately, we lost our top defender against Berkeley. They had a lot of dangerous stick swings, and an ejection, and four or five yellow cards, We will have a discussion with the referees before the game and ask Berkeley’s coaches to watch for dangerous checks. During the game, our kids began fearing for their safety, so that put jitters into them because they were afraid to get hurt. If things start getting chippy, we’ll call a timeout and bring the refs and coaches together to make sure we’re staying safe,” said Chan, who has won every WACC banner since entering the league in 2019. After losing to BOD 7-6 on March 18, the Highlanders have extra motivation to win. But first they must get past Berkeley. “We aren’t even mentioning O’Dowd right now. Our focus is Berkeley and we’ll prep for O’Dowd when the time comes,” said Chan. 15-11 win over Berkeley The Highlanders led 10-7 by halftime but had to rally from a 5-2 deficit with 13 minutes remaining in the half. Piedmont added a goal from Ruby Guzdar and Katherine Kinne two minutes later to make it 5-4. Berkeley scored once before halftime but wouldn’t score again until 40 seconds were left. Charlotte Theut scored make it 6-5 and Photos by Todd Marshburn Elizabeth Ethington had three goals and seven assists vs. Berkeley. Kinne tied the match at 6-6, and PHS ahead 7-6 with 4:55 left in the half. Kinne scored again, and Eleanor Lavin boosted Piedmont’s lead to 9-6. Berkeley scored with 40 seconds left, but PHS added another on the very next possession by Kinne. In the second half, PHS came out with goals by Kinne and Elizabeth Ethington in the first five minutes for a 12-7 advantage. Berkeley made it 12-8 with 15 minutes to go but didn’t score again for 11 minutes. The Highlanders, meanwhile, added goals by Molly Ashton, Kinne, and Elizabeth Ethington. With Piedmont safely in control, Berkeley scored three times in the final five minutes of action. Final stats: Kinne scored seven goals and two assists. Elizabeth Ethington had three goals and seven assists. Theut scored twice. Lavin, Ashton, and Guzdar had individual goals. Goalies Sophia Ethington had six saves in the first half while Lindsay Kottle had eight saves. 10-7 win over Acalanes The Highlanders were well ahead of Acalanes by halftime, leading 7-2, but allowed the Dons to get closer before closing it out at 10-7. Final stats: Theut scored four goals with one assist. Kinne scored twice with two assists. Elizabeth Ethington had one goal and four assists. Audrey Mahany scored twice. Molly Ashton scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-8 overall, 3-1 league) hosts Berkeley on Wednesday, April 27 at 7:00 p.m. at Witter Field in a double-header with the PHS boys’ team. With a victory, they would host the WACC Championship game, likely with Bishop O’Dowd, on Friday, April 29 at 7:00 p.m. Piedmont prepares for the WACC Championship semifinals tonight with a rematch against Berkeley.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 27, 2022 13 Piedmont lacrosse team heads into WACC playoffs Staff Photos The PHS boys’ lacrosse team and coach Alex Yu look ahead to a rematch with Bishop O’Dowd in the league playoffs this week. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team split its last two games of the regular season, defeating Acalanes in overtime on Tuesday, April 19 in Lafayette, but losing to Novato 10-6 on Friday, April 22 at Witter Field. Both are considered top-level contenders in Division 2 of the North Coast Section. Piedmont was moved up to Div.1 in 2020 after winning the championship. “Novato and Acalanes are playing all Division 1 (opponents), and they are Div.2, explained Piedmont first-year head coach Alex Yu. “I’ve known Novato’s coach, Mike Hardy, since the old school, We played against each other back in 88’-89.” The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 7-7 overall, second to O’Dowd in the WACC with a 4-1 record against league opponents. The Dragons won their regular season match 13-7 on March 18. The Highlanders will receive a first-round bye as the No. 2 seed, and will play No. 3 Berkeley (12- 9) today, April 27 at 5:30 p.m. Witter Field is the host site for this year’s championship game on Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont has won every WACC Championship since entering the league in 2017 but faces stiff competition from a strong O’Dowd team. “We’ll see Berkeley on Wednesday and we don’t want to look past them. It’s one game at a time and we have to take care of business first,” said Yu. The Dragons enter the playoffs with the No. 1 seed for the first time since 2017. They defeated PHS 8-7 during the regular season, but the Highlanders went onto win the 2017 championship 9-8 in overtime. Yu was an assistant coach with O’Dowd on that team. 15-14 OT win over Acalanes It was a heated contest pm April 19 against the Dons of Acalanes. Piedmont trailed 5-4 by the end of the first quarter but went ahead 8-7 by halftime. The Dons stormed ahead with five goals in the third quarter to take a 12-10 lead. In the fourth quarter, PHS scored four goals to jump ahead, 14-13 with 1:21 left in the game. Acalanes tied the match with 36 seconds left to play to force overtime. In OT, the Highlanders were able to kill a 90-second penalty, and Jack Nelson scored the game-winner in the closing minutes. Midfielder Noah Lindenbaum was awarded the game ball after recording a pivotal clearance in overtime that changed possession and helped Piedmont win the game. Final stats: Nate Fredericks led with six goals and one assist. Soren Dixon had four goals and four assists. Spencer Settlemier scored twice. Jack Nelson had two goals and an assist. Rylan Nelson scored once. 10-6 loss to Novato Novato came out the gates with a 5-1 lead in the first quarter and 7-2 by halftime. Piedmont narrowed the score to 7-4 in the third period, but a 3-goal deficit was the closest it got, ending in a 10-6 win for Novato. Final stats: Fredericks scored twice with two ground balls. Dixon had a goal, assist, and a ground ball. Jack Nelson scored once with six ground balls. Berkeley made it 12-8 with 15 minutes to go but didn’t score again for 11 minutes. The Highlanders, meanwhile, added goals by Molly Ashton, Kinne, and Elizabeth Ethington. articles.text: Wilson Wong had eight spikes against Encinal. The PHS volleyball team is contending for its first North Coast Section playoff berth in its first year of eligibility. The Highlanders defeated Encinal 3-1 on Thursday, April 21 at home and now have a league record of 5-6. Prior to Thursday’s match, the Highlanders honored their four seniors: Mason Kimball, Felix Broach, Atom Rognuson, and Adel Sahuc. Piedmont was able to allow some players to play different positions. “It was really fun to let Felix move to the back row, because he’s a middle and never plays there,’ said coach Mariah Cardenas. “He made our last kill to win the game, so it was really fun to watch. If we can win the next two matches, we can go to the next portion [post-season playoffs].” To qualify for the playoffs, PHS must finish with a .500 overall record, league record, or record against Div. 3 NCS teams. Given that all Piedmont’s matches have been against WACC opponents, the basis of qualifying could be their results against Div. 3 teams; PHS is now 2-2 against divisional opponents following Thursday’s win over the Jets. “If we can win the next two matches, we’ll be assured to get into the playoffs. The goal is to go into the matches strong, we want to shake off the jitters early and shake off the dust from spring break, and continue to take this season into playoffs,” said Cardenas. With a season-finale against Alameda, a D2 school which PHS beat 3-1 in the season-opener on March 8, the Highlanders are looking to officially punch their ticket to NCS. “The focus is to win. We need to win to make NCS [playoffs] so all focus in practice and games has to be there. We lost the first set against Encinal, and we can’t let something like that happen again,” said senior leader Mason Kimball. 3-1 win over Encinal The Highlanders dropped the first set 25-17 after starting the match with some reserve players on the floor. PHS powered back in the second set to win 25-21, won 25-22 in the third set, and finished with a dominant 25-14 fourth set. In the second set, Encinal opened with three of the first four points but PHS went ahead 5-4 and never relinquished the lead. The Highlanders held its largest lead at 20-10 and were able to bring in some reserves, once again. At 23-21, James MaNugyen slammed down backto-back spikes to win. In the third set, Encinal opened with three straight points, but the Highlanders reclaimed the lead at 5-4 and never conceded their advantage. Encinal began a comeback while trailing 23-16, narrowing the gap to 23-20 and 24-22, but a Jets’ offensive attempt going into the net closed it 25-22. In the fourth game, the win was never in doubt. Encinal held a 4-3 lead briefly, but Piedmont went on multiple scoring runs to extend their lead to 17-9. The Highlanders got the final five points thanks to Jets’ defense being out of rotational position to draw instant penalties. Broach got the winning kill, 25-14. Final stats: Wilson Wong Staff Photo Mason Kimball had five kills and four aces against the Jets. Staff Photo had eight kills and an ace. Kimball had five kills and four aces. Broach had three kills. PHS volleyball fighting for playoff spot By Jonathan Comeaux The PHS volleyball team is contending for its first North Coast Section playoff berth in its first year of eligibility. The Highlanders defeated Encinal 3-1 on Thursday, April 21 at home and now have a league record of 5-6. Prior to Thursday’s match, the Highlanders honored their four seniors: Mason Kimball, Felix Broach, Atom Rognuson, and Adel Sahuc. Piedmont was able to allow some players to play different positions. “It was really fun to let Felix move to the back row, because he’s a middle and never plays there,’ said coach Mariah Cardenas. “He made our last kill to win the game, so it was really fun to watch. If we can win the next two matches, we can go to the next portion [post-season playoffs].” To qualify for the playoffs, PHS must finish with a .500 overall record, league record, or record against Div. 3 NCS teams. Given that all Piedmont’s matches have been against WACC opponents, the basis of qualifying could be their results against Div. 3 teams; PHS is now 2-2 against divisional opponents following Thursday’s win over the Jets. “If we can win the next two matches, we’ll be assured to get into the playoffs. The goal is to go into the matches strong, we want to shake off the jitters early and shake off the dust from spring break, and continue to take this season into playoffs,” said Cardenas. With a season-finale against Alameda, a D2 school which PHS beat 3-1 in the season-opener on March 8, the Highlanders are looking to officially punch their ticket to NCS. “The focus is to win. We need to win to make NCS [playoffs] so all focus in practice and games has to be there. We lost the first set against Encinal, and we can’t let something like that happen again,” said senior leader Mason Kimball. 3-1 win over Encinal The Highlanders dropped the first set 25-17 after starting the match with some reserve players on the floor. PHS powered back in the second set to win 25-21, won 25-22 in the third set, and finished with a dominant 25-14 fourth set. In the second set, Encinal opened with three of the first four points but PHS went ahead 5-4 and never relinquished the lead. The Highlanders held its largest lead at 20-10 and were able to bring in some reserves, once again. At 23-21, James MaNugyen slammed down backto-back spikes to win. articles.text: Conductor Gustavo Dudamel let San Francisco Symphony in Mahler’s masterful Symphony No. 5 Guest conductor Gustavo Dudamel was back with gusto, leading “this foaming, roaring, raging sea of sound,” as Mahler once described his own raging Symphony No. 5. The Venezuelan led with fire – and no printed score – through this 71-minute masterpiece that Mahler’s compatriots in Vienna would call “gefühlsmȁssig” – surfeited with emotion. The crowd at Davies Hall stayed hushed in awe, without fidget or distraction, in hearing a master at work with the virtuoso San Francisco Symphony. Until the patrons’ jubilant ovations at the end. Often lost in all the flames and embers of this night is the clarity and articulation of strings, one result of the conductor’s early violin studies. This refinement was already evident in the Mozart Symphony No. 38 (“Prague”) that went just prior, with a far smaller orchestra (devoid of Mahler’s army, which added trombones, cymbals, clarinets, harp, tuba, bass drum). Under Dudamel, this was a virtuoso orchestra, prepped as if going on tour. If Beethoven had the definitive Fifth for the 19th century, Mahler produced his own for the 20th century. This vast Fifth from 1902 runs the gamut from keys in the funereal minor mode, on a scale like Verdi’s, to the ultra-serene Adagietto for strings (these days the most often excerpted Mahler selection). Then onto a playful and exuberant final movement where, if anything, the heavens appear to open up, suggesting perhaps that all is well after all. Quite simply, every one has feelings. But Mahler had them ever more intensely, high drama all the way, from groveling despair to unsurpassed exultation, and was able to set them to music with his vast musical forces. Working without a score, Dudamel was unafraid to let them all ring out. Today he occupies a unique position among Latin American podium figures, creating not only great music but also recognized as one of the most important music educators (via El Sistema) of recent decades. There were many highlights, from the opening growling basses simulating earthquakes up to the flutes and the shimmering trumpet solos of Mark Inouye. And in between, the softest pianissimos of which strings are ever capable. And did we mention the exquisite crescendos, the chattering woodwinds, and the versatility of Robert Ward and his horn section, at times with bells turned upward to provide a more country-village sound? The focus and intensity from the podium waned only in the finale – mobile, but less engrossing. The April 21 program had opened with the Mozart Symphony No. 38 in which the brass vied to be dominant. Consummate refinement, with the roars all held back till later. MUSIC NOTES – Dudamel, now in his 40s, led throughout from memory. He may have been the shortest man on stage, but once again, he stood tall. This was a rare Northern California appearance, as he also leads the L.A. Philharmonic on a heavy schedule. Also one year ago he was named the music director of the Paris Opera, a surprise venture given his heavy symphonic immersion over the years. SAN FRANCISCO SYMPHONY with guest Gustavo Dudamel on the podium in Mahler, Mozart, through April 24. For info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www.sfsymphony.org. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, has been a SF Bay Area classical-music critic for years.

Conductor Gustavo Dudamel let San Francisco Symphony in Mahler’s masterful Symphony No. 5 By Paul Hertelendy Guest conductor Gustavo Dudamel was back with gusto, leading “this foaming, roaring, raging sea of sound,” as Mahler once described his own raging Symphony No. 5. The Venezuelan led with fire – and no printed score – through this 71-minute masterpiece that Mahler’s compatriots in Vienna would call “gefühlsmȁssig” – surfeited with emotion. The crowd at Davies Hall stayed hushed in awe, without fidget or distraction, in hearing a master at work with the virtuoso San Francisco Symphony. Until the patrons’ jubilant ovations at the end. Often lost in all the flames and embers of this night is the clarity and articulation of strings, one result of the conductor’s early violin studies. This refinement was already evident in the Mozart Symphony No. 38 (“Prague”) that went just prior, with a far smaller orchestra (devoid of Mahler’s army, which added trombones, cymbals, clarinets, harp, tuba, bass drum). Under Dudamel, this was a virtuoso orchestra, prepped as if going on tour. If Beethoven had the definitive Fifth for the 19th century, Mahler produced his own for the 20th century. This vast Fifth from 1902 runs the gamut from keys in the funereal minor mode, on a scale like Verdi’s, to the ultra-serene Adagietto for strings (these days the most often excerpted Mahler selection). Then onto a playful and exuberant final movement where, if anything, the heavens appear to open up, suggesting perhaps that all is well after all. Quite simply, every one has feelings. But Mahler had them ever more intensely, high drama all the way, from groveling despair to unsurpassed exultation, and was able to set them to music with his vast musical forces. Working without a score, Dudamel was unafraid to let them all ring out. Today he occupies a unique position among Latin American podium figures, creating not only great music but also recognized as one of the most important music educators (via El Sistema) of recent decades. There were many highlights, from the opening growling basses simulating earthquakes up to the flutes and the shimmering trumpet solos of Mark Inouye. And in between, the softest pianissimos of which strings are ever capable. And did we mention the exquisite crescendos, the chattering woodwinds, and the versatility of Robert Ward and his horn section, at times with bells turned upward to provide a more country-village sound? The focus and intensity from the podium waned only in the finale – mobile, but less engrossing. The April 21 program had opened with the Mozart Symphony No. 38 in which the brass vied to be dominant. Consummate refinement, with the roars all held back till later. MUSIC NOTES – Dudamel, now in his 40s, led throughout from memory. He may have been the shortest man on stage, but once again, he stood tall. This was a rare Northern California appearance, as he also leads the L.A. Philharmonic on a heavy schedule. Also one year ago he was named the music director of the Paris Opera, a surprise venture given his heavy symphonic immersion over the years. SAN FRANCISCO SYMPHONY with guest Gustavo Dudamel on the podium in Mahler, Mozart, through April 24. For info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www.sfsymphony.org. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, has been a SF Bay Area classical-music critic for years.

articles.text: The Revenant is an extraordinary film: intense, unrelenting, gorgeous to behold and unflinching in its realism. The year is 1823. It’s mid-winter in Montana and South Dakota. A group of men, working for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company, are just completing six months of trapping, preparing pelts and readying their riverboat for a return trip to their basecamp, a roughly constructed fort downstream. The trip will be long and arduous. The forest is quiet, wind stirs high in the trees when suddenly a man, in mid-sentence, is shot in the throat by an arrow. The group is set upon by Arikara warriors, and the trappers must fight a desperate and brutal battle as they attempt to get to the boat and escape. Among the few survivors are Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his son, Hawk (Forrest Goodluck), who is part Pawnee. During one of their stops along the way Glass is attacked by a grizzly sow, protecting her cubs. It is one of the most heart-stopping scenes in the film, a mauling that leaves Glass close to death. The party makes the decision to leave behind three men, including Hawk, to bury Glass when he dies (they are certain he is near death) and then make the journey on their own to the fort. His son, killed by one of the trappers, Glass – still alive – is thrown into a shallow grave and partially buried. Through sheer will, he eventually emerges, discovers the body of his dead son, and thus begins what will be a 200-mile journey across some of the coldest and unforgiving landscape imaginable. His mission is to find the men who were responsible: John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy), a ruthless, mercenary man, and a young, unsuspecting neophyte, Jim Bridger (Will Poulter). Simply put, this is a story of vengeance, privation and endurance. What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – it will take your breath away – and the crucible Leonardo DiCaprio stars in The Revenant. of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (“Birdman”), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. Having said that, the acting is also superb, for it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they, like their characters, endured as they struggled to survive what proved to be a long and grueling shoot. Clearly they, along with Lubezki and Inarritu, will be recognized by the Oscars for what is a beautiful and difficult story to watch. Film can be art and both director and cinematographer have given us a gift, a primeval story, elegant in its simplicity yet framed by sublime moments of pain. The film won Academy awards for DiCaprio as Best Actor in a leading role, for Alejandro González Iñárritu as Best Director, and Emmanuel Lubezki for Best Cinematography. The Revenant. Directed by Alejandro Gonzalez Innarritu. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Tom Hardy, Domhall Gleeson. 2 hrs., 36 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Honey Boy is a raw, gritty, semi-autobiographical film, released in 2019, written by Shia LaBeouf wherein he reveals a period in his life when he was living in a seedy L.A. motel with his father, who he names James Lort (LaBeouf). His two alterego characters are 12-year-old Otis (Noah Jupe), a child actor, and the twenty-something, Otis (Chris Hedges) who has become a self-destructive movie star ordered into rehab by a judge. It’s in rehab, during sessions with a therapist, that Otis tells his story in a series of long flashbacks. The year is 1995. James, as becomes quickly evident, is not so much a father as a man locked in perpetual battle with his own demons, while young Otis struggles to avoid becoming collateral damage. James – an alcoholic, ex-con, veteran, and former rodeo clown – riffs and rants and rages, his verbal abuse of Otis on occasion turns physical. Their interaction pretty much takes place in the confines of their motel room, usually before James takes Otis to the set on his motorcycle or in the evening when they have returned to their claustrophobic room. James is ostensibly managing Otis’ career as a child star acting in B-movies. And while Otis is on set, James attends AA meetings, veterans therapy groups, or plants rows of marijuana along a nearby freeway. Their dysfunctional relationship is that of father and son; however, it’s also one in which the son assumes the role of the reasonable adult and the father becomes the unreasonable child. There are times when Otis hates his father, the man who has exposed him to alcohol, weed, and cigarettes, seems to relish denigrating him while demeaning the size of his pre-adolescent penis. He meets and then tosses Otis’ Big Brother/mentor into the motel pool. He often rides off on his Harley, leaving Otis to spend long nights fending for himself. But then Otis also loves his father, craves his attention, and wants above all to be wrapped in his arms and protected. Regardless, James seems only intent on transferring to Otis – a lonely, precocious boy – the gnarled and twisted damage likely visited upon him. Honey Boy is not a vanity project by LaBeouf; rather, it’s a bleak, personal psychological dive into a complex relationship that haunts both father and son. If James is addicted to rage and chaos (now that he’s no longer drinking), Otis is addicted to his need to be loved by this tortured man. The performances of all three actors (LaBeouf, Jupe and Hedges) are astonishingly good. As is this strangely named film, Honey Boy. Honey Boy. Directed by Alma Har’el. Starring Shia LaBeouf, Lucas Hedges and Noah Jupe. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Lucas Hedges, Shia LaBeouf and Noah Jupe (front) star in Honey Boy.

articles.text: Mud, released in 2013, is a remarkable coming-of-age film about two boys, Ellis (Tye Sheridan) and Neckbone (Jacob Lofland) who live on the Mississippi River, Ellis in a water’s edge wooden shack with his increasingly estranged parents (Ray McKinnon and Sarah Paulson). His mother, who has lived on the river all of her life, yearns to move to town. His father, a stern fisherman, stubbornly resists. Ellis declares that he too loves the river and never wants to be a “townie,” and increasingly feels the tension that exists between his parents. Written and directed by Jeff Nichols, Mud begins with Ellis and Neckbone, having heard of a motorboat wedged high up in a tree during a violent storm, and using Ellis’ flat-bottomed riverboat, motor out to a small island to investigate. To their surprise they find the tree and climb up to investigate the boat. As they inspect the interior, they discover that someone is living on board. That person turns out to be a man who calls himself Mud (Matthew McConaughy). Clearly he’s a drifter, and explains that he is living on the boat, but if the boys will help bring him some food, he’ll give them the boat. He later reveals that he is a fugitive wanted for murder, and is waiting to be reunited with his girlfriend, the love of his life, called Juniper (Reese Witherspoon). She’s in town, he explains, staying in a motel, waiting. Ellis, on the cusp of full-blown adolescence, his hormones swirling, is caught up in Mud’s romantic story, and despite Neckbone’s skepticism, is intent on helping Mud, first with food and later with tools and rope (to lower the motorboat) and an engine. Meanwhile Ellis crushes on a local girl, May Pearl (Bonnie Sturdivant), two grades ahead of Ellis and to his confusion flirts with him while rejecting him when her friends are nearby. As the boys soon learn, not only is Mud hiding out from the law, but from bounty hunters, hired by King, the father (Joe Don Baker) of the man that Mud killed trying to protect Juniper. Ellis is undaunted and tells Neckbone that they should do whatever they can to help Mud and Juniper. Jeff Nichols’ screenplay is part mystery, fable, and thriller, and is, in the imagination of both Ellis and Mud, a love story. Clearly, Mud can be called a Southern Gothic tale, as much about its authentic characters as about place and language. It rings true in all respects. As a story, it is in the best tradition of Tennessee Williams and Mark Twain. It is also a noir metaphor for how a newbie teen copes with the imminent divorce of his parents, who have grown disenchanted with the idea of loving one another. All of this leads to a satisfying, but violent act three that ends with a twist. Mud, Written and directed by Jeff Nichols. Starring Matthew McConaughy, Reese Witherspoon, Tye Sheridan, and Jacob Lofland. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Tubi/Amazon Prime. We arrived at the dock five minutes after the scheduled departure. The first words we heard from the ticket taker were, “Relax, the ship is waiting for you.” Yep, you guessed it, they held ship for us. The boat was an old-fashioned paddlewheeler and the musical show was an extravaganza. All of the entertainers were first rate musicians and singers. Many of them had impressive solos. For the pure musical value, the show was exceptional. But everything these days needs a large dose of glitz. The entertainers changed their outfits after every number. I thought it unnecessary, but the public screamed vociferously. As I watched the audience, they seemed to know the words to every song. Even the junior high school kids knew the words to the songs. Enthusiasm was everywhere. As I walked on the deck of the General Jackson paddlewheeler, I was reminded of a great story. In the 1840s the Norwegian-American violinist Ole Bull was very popular in America. He was a big, muscular and handsome man, and looked kind of like a violin-playing version of Arnold Schwarzenegger. While Bull was walking on deck, a man came up behind him demanding his money. The violinist turned around, picked up the robber, and threw him into the river. And that is a true story. This being Nashville, music is everywhere. At breakfast, I heard the people at the table next to me talking about music. The names were a veritable Who’s Who of country stars. There was Minnie Pearl, Tex Ritter, Conway Twitty, Waylon Jennings, and of course Elvis. The Nashville sound deserves its reputation. articles.text: Lee Cliff, co-founder of the Piedmont 4th of July Parade in 1965 and its first Uncle Sam, peacefully passed away on March 20, 2022 in Cupertino surrounded by family members. Born Lee Harker Cliff on August 7, 1930, he was the son of Frank and Margaret Cliff. Lee graduated from Palo Alto High School in 1948, and Dartmouth College in 1952. He served in the U.S. Army from 1952-1955, attending the Army Language School in Monterey, and then stationed in Japan, Korea, and the Philippines. After the service Lee earned his Law degree from UC Berkeley School of Law in 1958, and practiced law in San Francisco at Hall, Henry, Oliver and Mcreavy until the mid 1980s. He then worked as a legal mediator before settling into full retirement. In the years in which he lived in Piedmont, he and a close friend Dick Johnson decided that the city needed to have its own 4th of July Parade, so they created one in 1965. Johnson was then on the Recreation Commission, and with the tall, lean Lee Cliff, he had the ideal Uncle Sam for the parade. “My dad and Lee were super close friends,” explained Kathy Kelleher, the daughter of parade co-founder Dick Johnson. The Johnsons and the Cliffs were great family friends and vacationed together. “We did a big crepe paper float of the American flag on a Piedmont 4th of July Parade founders Dick Johnson (left) and Lee Cliff. Lee Cliff leads the Piedmont 4th of July Parade as Uncle Sam. flatbed trailer. The trailer was hooked up to a pickup truck and Nell Cliff (as Betsy Ross) was hand-sewing American Flags in the back of the truck. Lee was at the front leading the parade as Uncle Sam. “All the neighborhood kids could hardly wait for our dads to come home from work, because we worked on the floats as a neighborhood in the evenings.” On August 12, 1955 Lee married Nell Sesnon, with whom he spent his life until she passed away in November 2021. They raised four children in Piedmont and then moved to Santa Cruz where they were active in the community for 30 years. Lee and Nell lived their last 11 years at The Forum at Rancho San Antonio in Santa Clara County. Lee enjoyed photography, bread making, woodworking, and making wine from chardonnay grapes that he grew. He was an avid reader, and enjoyed Dixieland and bluegrass music. Above all, Lee loved thoughtful conversation with anyone who would participate. He was intelligent, knowledgeable and had a strong sense of fairness. Lee is predeceased by his wife, Nell Sesnon Cliff, daughter Molly Cliff Hilts, and brother Frank B. Cliff. He is survived by his children Dan (Martha) Cliff, Susan Cliff, Peter (Sheila) Cliff, his son-in-law Dave Hilts, six grandchildren, and many nieces and nephews. Memorial contributions may be made to the Equal Justice Initiative (www.eji.org), a non-profit founded by social justice activist Brian Stevenson.

articles.text: Joan Beamer Metcalf, a lifelong resident of Piedmont, passed away at home on April 15, 2022, at the age of 81. She will be greatly missed. Born in Oakland, California on September 6, 1940, she was the daughter of Scott and Alpha Mae Beamer and the oldest of five children. In her youth, Joan attended Havens Elementary School and Piedmont High School before enrolling in San Francisco State University. Joan raised a family of four children in Piedmont. She was always available to her children and lavished love and attention on her grandchildren. Joan was an organizer and planner, and a renowned hostess with a reputation for entertaining and creating wonderful gatherings. Her door was always open, and her greatest joy was gathering people together. From football team banquets to birthday parties to family holiday dinners, friends and family were welcomed to her home for festive events and unforgettable meals. The table was full when friends were there. Joan was a devoted mother and a generous gourmet cook who was known for her famous toffee recipe. She loved sunshine and enjoyed traveling, reading fiction and cookbooks, and tending her garden. She loved her family above all else and took pride in her children and grandchildren, cherishing time spent with them on vacations, at their athletic events, school performances, and in the family home – an unofficial Piedmont landmark. Much of her time was spent in the service of others, and she taught her children and grandchildren selflessness as she gave her time to schools, Campfire Girls and Cub Scouts. She found fulfillment from her membership and leadership in a variety of charitable organizations Lifelong Piedmont resident Joan Metcalf died on April 15 at age 81. and developed great friendships during her years of volunteer work. She was a long-time member of Hollyhocks for Lincoln Child Center, and Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland with time and energy contributed to The Winter Ball. The entire family had many happy years attending the Ball together. More recently, Joan was active in Home Gardeners and relished their field trips. She had a passion for the Oakland Museum of California and was a member of The Oakland Museum Women’s Board since 1978. She was an ardent supporter of the White Elephant Sale, chairing the Household Department for many years. Her organizational skills found a home in sorting merchandise, and she and her mother, Alpha Mae Beamer, were a dynamic team in the years they worked together. Joan further brought her love of planning and hosting events to these groups by opening her home to annual parties and celebrations that became traditions for her friends. Joan will be missed by her four siblings, her four children, and six grandchildren. Her life will be celebrated in a private service for family. She started the transformation of her yard, planting natives that now dominate. There are over 50 species of native trees and shrubs that provide food, cover, and homes for native insects, bees, birds, butterflies and more, including several species of native Californian oaks. These trees are considered a “keystone” species because of the vast number of animals which they support, numbering in the low hundreds. In lieu of a conventional lawn, Hope has established a native wildflower meadow of deep-rooted native grasses that prevent soil erosion and feed native wildlife mixed with perennial and annual re-seeding wildflowers. When grasses go to seed, the seedhead is actually the flower of the grass plant. Some of the plants have edible flowers, and Hope provided Tami DeSellier with some samples. In 2016, Hope’s garden qualified as a Certified Monarch Waystation with areas planted in native milkweed, the sole food plant for the Monarchs in their pre-chrysalis larval form. Hope is thrilled to see Monarch caterpillars and butterflies enjoying her garden every year. Hope also told the group of her efforts to live a sustainable, carbon-neutral life with her family in their home. During the winters they wear layers inside the house, and keep the thermostat temperature in the upper fifties. The family is also conscious of minimizing the carbon associated with their travel. After the visit and tour of her garden, the walkers retraced their steps back to the Community Hall parking lot. A second passenger was cited for possession of methamphetamine, delaying police, but was taken to the hospital due to injuries.
